why: The structural invariants of a loaded model are checked three times: by the
engine in packages/zig/scene-runner/src/structure.zig, by the TypeScript host in
packages/ts/scene-runner/src/validate-model.ts, and earlier and against source by
the Go compiler in packages/go/converter/internal/validate. The host's copy is a
convenience -- a synchronous ModelValidationError before any engine call -- not a
second opinion. The compiler's is the one that can point at a line.
Three copies of one rule set is exactly the shape every other shared name in this
repository is gated against: field types, function aliases, the runtime projection,
the model versions, the shared bounds. This one was not. The wording in the engine
and host files is identical, which is what a port looks like, and nothing failed
when they disagreed -- the host rejected a valueless binding that a prepare entry
fills while the engine ran it, and no test on either side noticed.
So: `shared` is what the engine and host must both enforce, and `hostOnly` is what
the host adds on purpose. A rule in neither list, appearing in either file, is drift.
`compiler` then maps each shared rule onto the Go diagnostic that catches it at
compile time. The compiler was left out of this file at first, on the grounds that
its diagnostics carry error codes and source positions and are worded for an author
looking at a .tu file rather than for a host handed a model. That is true of the
*wording*, and this section does not gate wording -- it gates existence. Leaving it
ungated cost exactly what the rest of the file was written to prevent: `route "x"`
declared twice compiled clean and produced a model the engine refused to load,
reported against no file and no line, and the same was true of a route taking a
scene's name. Both now have compiler codes, and a shared rule with neither a `code`
nor an `unreachable` reason fails this gate.

shared.why: Two scenes with one id make every reference to it ambiguous.
Two routes with one id make dispatch by entryId ambiguous.
entryId resolves against both namespaces, so a shared id is ambiguous.
A route with no entry scene has nowhere to start.
The entry scene must be present before the run begins; unlike a match target, it cannot arrive from an extend hook later.
A transition to a scene that does not exist cannot be taken. Suppressed when the model declares an extend hook, because the target may still arrive.
Two actions with one id make every next rule naming it ambiguous.
A scene whose entry action does not exist cannot start.
The root names the binding whose value is the action's result.

A binding with no value, no expression and no prepare entry can never hold anything. The prepare schedule is part of the rule: a binding filled from STATE, a hook, or an earlier action legitimately carries neither.

why: The engine warns and carries on: fixtures/scene-route-vectors.json pins it,
in 'post-merge state and action output', which merges a binding called
`absent`. The TypeScript host rejects it as a likely typo. That is a host
judgement about what to hand its callers, which spec/runtime-hosts.md leaves
to the host — it is not a claim that the engine cannot run the model.
The engine warns and carries on: fixtures/scene-route-vectors.json pins it,
in 'conditional action and wildcard route', which routes past a rule
targeting `never`. Rejected by the host for the same reason as above.

rules.unreachable: The compiler builds the binding rather than reading one. lower_rhs.go writes either a value or an expr and never both, so there is no source that produces this shape and nothing for a diagnostic to report against. It stays a load-time check because a model can also arrive hand-written or from another compiler.
